extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political theory; legislators; philosophers; readers of classical political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for classifying, designing, and assessing constitutions and political regimes (kingship, aristocracy, oligarchy, democracy, tyranny), with attention to which persons, laws, and social conditions make a government good or corrupt. Emphasises matching laws and institutions to the character and composition of a city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy of law over individual will
rubrics_metrics.description: Law is reason without desire; it is preferable that supreme power be placed in the laws (and in the mind as embodied by law) rather than in fallible men whose passions influence them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws provide impartiality and continuity; entrusting supreme power to individuals risks passion-driven decisions even by good men. The legislator should aim to place the highest authority in law where possible, altering particulars by experience but keeping law as the guiding, desire-free standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law must allow practical adjustment and be experience-responsive
rubrics_metrics.description: While laws express general principles, they should permit adjustment and alteration where experience shows improvement is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws should be drafted with room for magistrates' discretion in particulars and for amendment when practical outcomes indicate change is beneficial; rigid universal prescriptions that cannot be improved by experience are unsuitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of self-partiality via external judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who judge themselves or their friends are prone to partiality; impartial judgment often requires recourse to external authorities or multiple judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to medicine: when a physician is suspected of bias, patients consult books or other physicians. Similarly, magistrates should have mechanisms (appeal, multiple judges, rotation) to mitigate self-interest and partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of decision-makers is preferable to sole rule
rubrics_metrics.description: For cases not fully covered by written law it is better that many decide than a single person; many can 'see' and 'hear' better collectively than one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions with multiple magistrates or councils rather than concentrating discretionary power in one individual; delegation and broad participation reduce error and abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match governmental form to the nature of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: Different men by nature are fit for different forms (some for slavery under a master, some for monarchy, some for a free state); tyranny and perverted forms are contrary to nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the natural dispositions, customs, and character of a polity's people when choosing a constitution; what is 'best' is relative to the population's nature and capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is fit to rule: criteria for kingly, aristocratic, democratic rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Kingly rule should be for those accustomed to submit civil government to a family eminent for virtue; aristocracy for those framed to bear the rule of free men by superior virtue; a free state for a war-like people formed to govern and be governed by laws admitting even the poorest to honours when merited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social dispositions and prevailing virtues to determine which class or body should hold supreme power; specify which virtues or social arrangements justify each regime type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme power justified by genuine excellence/virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: If a family or individual so far excels in virtue as to exceed all others, it is right they should hold supreme power rather than be ostracised or rotate office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When genuine, exceptional excellence exists, institutional design may legitimately concentrate authority in that excellence rather than artificially limiting or rotating it; do not force superior persons into subordination contrary to nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and morals determine quality of citizens and rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Education and morals are almost the whole of what makes a good man; the same qualities make a good citizen and a good king.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise civic education and moral formation in institutional design; selection for offices should emphasise moral and educational qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislator must know both ideal and practical constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: A true legislator should be acquainted not only with the most perfect imaginable government but also with the best suited to given circumstances and how to preserve or correct existing governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft laws that are simple, attainable, and practically implementable; the legislator should be able to recognize theoretical best forms and feasible variants and to reform mistaken institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must be tailored to the state, not vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: All laws should be framed agreeable to the state that is to be governed, and not the state conformed to fixed laws; government (constitution) dictates what laws are appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the social composition, customs, and relations in a polity before imposing laws; avoid one-size-fits-all legal schemes divorced from local conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of democracy and oligarchy by holders of power
rubrics_metrics.description: A democracy is where the supreme power is in the hands of the freemen (the poor majority); an oligarchy is where the supreme power is in the hands of the rich (few).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify regimes by who actually holds political power (freemen vs rich), not merely by numerical majorities; consider eligibility rules, census, and social status when labelling regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between law-governed and vote-governed democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where democracy is governed by laws, it is a true free state; where decisions are driven by majoritarian votes and demagogues, the people rule with despotic power and resemble tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate democratic institutions on whether laws, rather than transient popular passions and leaders, hold supremacy; design safeguards (stable laws, institutions) against demagoguery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal composition determines number and species of governments
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities are composed of many parts (husbandmen, artificers, merchants, soldiers, rich, etc.); the differing ranks and occupations yield many different forms and species of governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the social, economic, and occupational structure of a polity to foresee which constitutional forms are feasible and which variations will arise; representation and offices should reflect necessary social functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential offices and self-sufficiency requirement for a city
rubrics_metrics.description: A city must be self-sufficient and include judge, council, military (men-at-arms) and those executing public offices; without these it cannot properly be a city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure institutions provide for justice, defence, public administration and provisioning; design eligibility and incentives so capable persons occupy these roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple species of democracy (classification criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different democracies exist: pure equality-based (law directs equality of rich/poor), census-based eligibility (small census but eligible within it), law-governed with only non-infamous citizens, universal citizen participation, and popular (vote-driven) democracies dominated by demagogues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing a democracy specify: eligibility rules, whether law or majority-vote is supreme, and mechanisms (wages, leisure) that enable participation; anticipate vulnerability to demagogues when assemblies are frequent and paid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple species of oligarchy (classification criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchies vary: offices regulated by property census; magistrates of small fortune self-filling offices; hereditary nobility; oligarchies not under law (dynasty), corresponding to tyrannies in monarchies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify oligarchies by the basis of office-holding (census, heredity, informal control) and by whether law restrains rulers; foresee transitions (wealth concentration → hereditary rule → dynasty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic conditions (leisure, wages, property distribution) shape regime form
rubrics_metrics.description: When citizens have leisure (moderate property) they govern according to law; when poor citizens receive wages and leisure, the poor may dominate and power may lodge with those who receive pay, leading to popular rule not in the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how public revenue, remuneration, and property distribution affect who can participate; design institutional incentives (remuneration, qualifications) to promote law-governed administration rather than paid, vote-driven manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuum and mixtures of regime types; aristocracy as ideal and variants
rubrics_metrics.description: True aristocracy is government by the best men on virtuous principles; other states mix elements (rich+virtuous+citizens) producing varieties such as virtuous democracies (e.g., Lacedaemon) or oligarchic tendencies within democracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise mixed regimes and hybrid features rather than insisting on pure labels; evaluate based on which principles (virtue, wealth, law, majority) dominate in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional sources of corruption and stability must be identified
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments will have particular sources of corruption and stability, some common to all forms and some peculiar to each; one should investigate these causes to preserve or reform regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or critiquing a constitution, diagnose structural vulnerabilities (concentration of wealth, demagoguery, hereditary claims) and stabilising features (laws, mixed participation, civic education) specific to that polity.
